{{Short description|Chess tournament series}}
{{distinguish|World Chess Championship}}

The '''FIDE World Cup''' is a major [[chess]] event organized by [[FIDE]], the international governing body of chess. 

==History==
Three different formats have been used:
*In 2000 and 2002, it was a [[multi-stage tournament]], with a [[group stage]] consisting of 24 players in four groups, followed by a [[knockout stage]].
*From 2005 to 2019, it was a biennial 128-player [[Single-elimination tournament|single-elimination]] tournament, forming part of the qualification for the [[World Chess Championship]].
*From the [[Chess World Cup 2021|2021 edition]] to the [[Chess World Cup 2025|2025 edition]], the number of players has increased to 206. A system of [[bye (tournament)|bye]]s is used in the first round; from the second round onwards the format is identical to the previous system.
*Beginning in 2027, the number of players will be increased to 224. Additionally, there will be two stages. The first one will be a swiss qualification, featuring four Swiss pools and nine rounds across five days. The second one will be a knockout finals, where 16 players qualified from the Swiss pools will play in a single-elimination tournament.

===Chess World Cup (1979)===
Before FIDE introduced the Chess World Cup, a tournament was organized in [[Montreal]] in 1979 under the name "World Cup". It was later renamed the "Man and his World Chess Challenge Cup" after the venue, [[Expo 67|Man and his World]].<ref name=":0">{{Cite book |last=Kavalek |first=Lubomir |author-link=Lubomir Kavalek |title=World Cup Chess: The Grand Masters' Grand Prix |publisher=Trafalgar Square Publishing |year=1990 |isbn=0-943955-31-9 |location=North Pomfret, Vermont |pages=11–12 |language=en}}</ref> The tournament was held as a [[double round-robin]] between ten leading grandmasters.<ref>{{Cite news |date=1979-04-11 |title=Karpov Heads a Field of 10 in Montreal Chess |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1979/04/11/archives/karpov-heads-a-field-of-10-in-montreal-chess.html |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200804005905/https://www.nytimes.com/1979/04/11/archives/karpov-heads-a-field-of-10-in-montreal-chess.html |archive-date=2020-08-04 |access-date=2026-02-13 |work=[[The New York Times]] |agency=Reuters}}</ref> [[Anatoly Karpov]] and [[Mikhail Tal]] shared first place after drawing each other in the final round.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Fontaine |first=Peter Alfred |title=Montreal 1979 |url=https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chesscollection?cid=1016901 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20260213172326/https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chesscollection?cid=1016901 |archive-date=2026-02-13 |access-date=2026-02-13 |website=chessgames.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Byrne |first=Robert |author-link=Robert Byrne (chess player) |date=1979-05-07 |title=Chess: Karpov and Tal Both Win Quebec's Chess Challenge |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1979/05/07/archives/chess-karpov-and-tal-both-win-quebecs-chess-challenge.html |url-status=live |access-date=2026-02-13 |work=[[The New York Times]]}}</ref>

===Chess World Cup (1988–1989)===
{{main|Chess World Cup 1988–1989}}
In 1988–1989, the Grandmasters Association (GMA), which had six players from the 1979 tournament as directors, organized six tournaments as the "[[Chess World Cup 1988–1989|GMA World Cup]]".<ref name=":0" /> Participants were high-ranking [[grandmaster (chess)|grandmaster]]s; each round was a large [[round-robin tournament|round robin]] termed a "Grand Prix". They were considered the flagship tournaments of the GMA but were abandoned as the association gradually collapsed in the early 1990s.<ref>[https://en.chessbase.com/post/garry-kasparov-a-history-of-profesional-che Garry Kasparov: A History of Profesional Chess], [[Mig Greengard]], [[Chessbase]], 4/8/2002</ref><ref>[https://www.chessgames.com/perl/chesscollection?cid=1015939 Skelleftea World Cup 1989], [[Chessgames.com]]</ref>

==FIDE World Cup (2000–2002)==

In 2000 and 2002 [[FIDE]], the International Chess Federation, staged their "First Chess World Cup" and "Second Chess World Cup" respectively. These were major tournaments, but not directly linked to the [[World Chess Championship]]. Both the [[Chess World Cup 2000|2000]]<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20010113232800/https://theweekinchess.com/html/twic306.html#2#2 The Week in Chess 306 (web archive)] 18 September 2000</ref> and [[Chess World Cup 2002|2002]]<ref>[https://web.archive.org/web/20090705224716/https://theweekinchess.com/html/twic415.html#3#3 The Week in Chess 415 (web archive)] 21 October 2002</ref> events were won by [[Viswanathan Anand]] of [[India]].

Both tournaments began with a round-robin stage, consisting of four groups of six players each. The top two players from each group were subsequently seeded into an eight-player single-elimination bracket.

== FIDE World Cup (2005–present) ==
{{See also|FIDE World Chess Championships (1998–2004)}}
Since 2005, a different event of the same name has been part of the World Chess Championship cycle. This event is being held every two years. It is a 128-player knockout tournament, in the same style as the [[Tilburg chess tournament|Tilburg tournament]] between 1992 and 1994, or the [[FIDE World Chess Championship 1998|1998]], [[FIDE World Chess Championship 1999|1999]], [[FIDE World Chess Championship 2000|2000]], [[FIDE World Chess Championship 2002|2002]] and [[FIDE World Chess Championship 2004|2004]] [[Chess World Championship|FIDE World Championships]].

The event was held in 2005, 2007, 2009, and 2011 in Khanty-Mansiysk, and subsequently FIDE has given preference to bids for the Olympiad that also contain a bid for the preceding World Cup.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.fide.com/component/content/article/1-fide-news/4195-bidding-procedure-for-the-chess-olympiad-2014.html |title=Bidding Procedure for 2014 Olympiad |access-date=2015-12-19 |archive-date=2015-12-22 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151222170736/http://www.fide.com/component/content/article/1-fide-news/4195-bidding-procedure-for-the-chess-olympiad-2014.html |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref>[https://www.fide.com/images/stories/NEWS_2012/Congress/Minutes_of_FIDE_General_Assembly_2012.pdf FIDE General Assembly Minutes (2012), section 18.5]</ref> During the 2015 finals of the World Cup, the main organizer commented "We received the right to host the Olympiad and then we were given an additional event – the World Cup."<ref>{{cite web |last1=Shafizade |first1=Sanan |title=Mahir Mammadov: "Armenian chess players don’t have and they won’t have any problems in Baku" |website=vestnikkavkaza.net |publisher=Vestnik Kavkaza |access-date=30 June 2025 |url=http://www.vestnikkavkaza.net/interviews/Mahir-Mammadov-Armenian-chess-players-don%E2%80%99t-have-and-they-won%E2%80%99t-have-any-problems-in-Baku.html |archive-date=17 October 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211017072043/http://www.vestnikkavkaza.net/interviews/Mahir-Mammadov-Armenian-chess-players-don%E2%80%99t-have-and-they-won%E2%80%99t-have-any-problems-in-Baku.html |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref>

The [[Chess World Cup 2005]] qualified ten players for the [[Candidates Tournament]] for the [[World Chess Championship 2007]]. Since then, every World Cup has qualified between one and three players for the Candidates Tournament.

Two World Cup qualifiers ([[Boris Gelfand]] in 2009 and [[Sergey Karjakin]] in 2015) won the subsequent Candidates tournament and played in the World Championship match, in [[World Chess Championship 2012|2012]] and [[World Chess Championship 2016|2016]] respectively.

===Format===
From 2005 to 2019, the format was 128 players with 7 single-elimination rounds of "mini-matches", which are 2 games each followed by a series of rapid then blitz tiebreaks if necessary. Since 2021, the World Cup has been expanded to 206 players playing 8 single-elimination rounds, with  50 players receiving a bye to the 2nd round.
The final usually has 4 games before the tiebreaks start. Since 2015, an extra rest day has recently been added before the semi-finals, in addition to before the final.<ref>[https://www.fide.com/FIDE/handbook/WorldCup2015Regulations.pdf World Cup 2015 Regulations]</ref>

Some criticism has been leveled at the scheduling effects, with the event being rather long (26 days), particularly with almost all of the players having left long before the end.<ref>[https://chess24.com/en/read/news/svidler-and-karjakin-on-the-world-cup-final-part-1 Svidler and Karjakin on the World Cup final] (Chess24)</ref> Fatigue thus plays a critical role, and while some players seek to conserve energy by avoiding tiebreaks, others "agree" (either explicitly or implicitly) to make short draws in the 2 long games and decide the winner in tiebreaks. It is often remarked that the system is mostly a lottery of who survives, though better players have more chances on the whole.<ref>[https://www.chess.com/article/view/chess-world-cup-2013-war-of-attrition Chess World Cup 2013, War of Attrition] (Chess.com)</ref> The anticlimax of the 4-round final, with both players now already qualified for the [[Candidates Tournament|Candidates]], has also been criticized.<ref>{{cite web |title=Александр Грищук: "В Тромсе была одна из худших организаций за очень долгое время" |url=http://chess-news.ru/node/13376 |website=chess-news.ru |access-date=30 June 2025 |archive-date=27 September 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210927192716/http://chess-news.ru/node/13376 |url-status=bot: unknown }}</ref>

===Winners===
"Qual" refers to the number of players who qualify for the [[Candidates Tournament]] (marked with green background). For example, in 2015, the top 2 finishers qualified for the [[2016 Candidates Tournament]]. In 2021, [[Sergey Karjakin]] qualified for the [[2022 Candidates Tournament]] via the World Cup, but was subsequently disqualified for making statements in support of the [[Russian invasion of Ukraine]]. In 2023, only the top three players were meant to qualify, but [[Magnus Carlsen]] declined to participate in the Candidates; thus the fourth place, [[Nijat Abasov]], qualified as well.
